title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the metaphor, the beat and the marks

questions.prompt: The first of the two texts calls genes the building blocks of nature. The phrase is not decoration — it is doing a piece of the arguing. What does it claim?

options.text: That everything rests on them, so a change low down can bring much down.
That genes are as hard and as difficult to break as stone is.
That genes were put in place by a designer, in the way that a building is.
That nature is a building site on which scientists are now at work.

questions.explanation: A building block is the smallest piece at the bottom of a wall, and everything above it stands on it. Calling genes the building blocks of nature therefore argues something precise: "That everything rests on them, so a change low down can bring much down." That is why the writer wants strict control rather than a ban — his fear is the size of the consequence, not the technique. "That genes are as hard and as difficult to break as stone is." takes the block for its material instead of its place. "That nature is a building site on which scientists are now at work." stretches the image to a term the writer never used. "That genes were put in place by a designer, in the way that a building is." turns a metaphor about structure into an argument about who built it, which the text does not make. Read every metaphor in an argumentative text as a claim, and then ask which claim exactly.

questions.prompt: You are reading the fifteen words of the module aloud and marking the beat in each one. Where does the beat fall in DVD?

options.text: evenly on all three, with no beat at all
on the first letter
on the last letter
on the middle letter

questions.explanation: A word spelt out letter by letter takes its beat on the last letter, so DVD is said D-V-**D**, and DNA beside it is said D-N-**A**. The same holds for initials outside this list: the U-S-**A**, an M-**P**. "on the first letter" applies the habit most of the rest of the list follows — INsulin, OPera, LAser, CONtact lenses — and these two words are exactly where that habit fails. "on the middle letter" puts the beat where English never puts it in a set of three initials. "evenly on all three, with no beat at all" describes no English word: one syllable always carries the beat, and here each letter is a syllable of its own.

questions.prompt: Two texts use the same hotel words. (1) "Our leisure club is open from seven, and our staff will book your treatments for you." (2) "Your leisure club was shut all week, and nobody would book anything for us." What tells you at once which of the two is the complaint?

options.text: The second is in the past, and its pronouns have changed sides.
The second is the shorter of the two, and a complaint is always short.
The second names the leisure club, while the first only hints at it.
The second uses the verb book, and that verb belongs to complaints.

questions.explanation: The two texts draw on one word list, so the vocabulary decides nothing; the tense and the pronouns decide everything. "The second is in the past, and its pronouns have changed sides." The brochure says our club and your treatments because the house is speaking to the guest; the complaint says your club and for us because the guest is now speaking to the house, and it puts the whole thing in the past because the week is over and cannot be mended. "The second uses the verb book, and that verb belongs to complaints." is wrong twice over: both texts use it, and no verb belongs to a genre. "The second names the leisure club, while the first only hints at it." is false on the page — both name it. "The second is the shorter of the two, and a complaint is always short." invents a rule, and a real letter of complaint is usually the longer of the two.

questions.prompt: A biography is printed as openings in one column and completions in another. One opening reads: "She won her first title after having ___". Which completion fits the grammar of that opening?

options.text: she trained for six years in a borrowed gym
train for six years in a borrowed gym
trained for six years in a borrowed gym
training for six years in a borrowed gym

questions.explanation: after having asks for a past participle, and nothing else: after having "trained for six years in a borrowed gym". Read the grammar of the opening before you read its meaning, and half the column matches itself. "train for six years in a borrowed gym" leaves the bare infinitive, which follows a modal and never follows having. "training for six years in a borrowed gym" doubles the -ing, and having is already carrying it. "she trained for six years in a borrowed gym" puts a whole clause with its own subject where a participle belongs, so the sentence would have two subjects and one verb too many. The same opening takes an object in front of the participle when somebody else acted: after having her application refused, she trained abroad.

questions.prompt: In one of these four sentences hopefully is the writer's own comment on the whole sentence, exactly as it is in the module's text. Which one?

options.text: Hopefully, the new treatment will be available next year.
She looked at the results hopefully and said nothing.
The doctors spoke hopefully about the coming trials.
The patients waited hopefully outside the consulting room.

questions.explanation: An -ly adverb that comments on the whole sentence stands at its head, cut off by a comma, and says what the writer thinks of what follows: "Hopefully, the new treatment will be available next year." means the writer hopes it will, and it says nothing at all about the treatment's own state of mind. In the three others the adverb has been pulled back beside a verb and describes the manner of an action instead — she looked hopefully, the doctors spoke hopefully, the patients waited hopefully — and there it is the people, not the writer, who are doing the hoping. That is the distinction to hold on to: at the head it is a comment, beside the verb it is a manner. And an adverb never describes the subject: if you mean the doctors themselves, you need the adjective, the doctors are hopeful.

questions.prompt: A pupil has typed this line with no capital letters at all: "in 1965 his country gave him the order of the republic in tunis and a film called silent harbour later told his story". Which of these must take a capital when the line is written properly?

options.text: in — the word the line opens on
country
order of the republic — the name of the award
tunis
silent harbour — the title of the film
story

questions.explanation: Four of the six take a capital. The line opens on in, and a sentence opens on a capital whatever kind of word stands there, prepositions included: In 1965. The award has an official name, and the naming words of it are proper nouns: the Order of the Republic — the little words of and the stay small. Tunis is a town, so it is a proper noun wherever it stands. And the title of a film keeps its capitals inside the sentence: a film called Silent Harbour. The two that stay small are the ones that describe instead of naming. country describes rather than names — Tunisia is the name, his country is not — exactly as a president and a world champion describe the people who hold those places. And story is a plain noun with nothing about it that is anybody's name: the film has a title, but his story does not.
